_readme: FACT ROYALE - THE FACT BASE
The unit of truth. A fact is a verified claim. A question is an
arrangement of facts. Rewording a question does not invalidate its
evidence, and one verified fact can serve many questions - including
refuting their distractors.
Full design and the reasoning behind every rule: docs/FACT-LAYER.md
SHARDING
Files are named by id block, never by tag, date or category.
A fact has no category - the QUESTION does. The same fact can back a
History question today and a Geography one tomorrow, so naming files
by category would bake in an association the data does not have.
The blocks are meaningless on purpose.
FIELDS
id           frq- for questions, fct- for facts. Permanent, never
positional, never a content hash.
claim        the verified assertion, in full. Self-contained: no
pronouns, no implied subject.
subject      the thing being asked about, as a noun phrase. Must NOT
contain the answer.
answer       the short answer string. Must appear in or be entailed
by the claim.
claimType    definition | point | enumeration | superlative | attribution
scope        REQUIRED for enumeration. What the list is complete over.
context      teaching prose. NOT a unit of verification. Anything in
here carrying real weight gets promoted to its own fact.
tags         2 to 4. Faceted vocabulary - see FACT-LAYER section 7.
era          plain convention, NOT ISO 8601. Negative means BC:
-399 is 399 BC. Null when there is no meaningful date.
riskTier     canonical | standard | volatile. Drives how many sources
are required.
volatility   static | slow | annual | seasonal | live. Drives recheck.
sources      ids into sources.json.
researchedBy may be claude.
approvedBy   MUST be a human. A fact without it cannot be published.
This is the guarantee that did not exist when the
question corpus was built.
supersededBy set when the WORLD changed. Edit instead when WE were
wrong. Superseded facts are kept for audit only: never
taught, never drawn, never cited by a new question.

facts.claim: About 90 percent of Madagascar's wildlife species are found nowhere else on Earth, including 92 percent of its mammals and 95 percent of its reptiles.
facts.subject: the share of Madagascar's wildlife found nowhere else on Earth
facts.context: Madagascar separated from the African mainland roughly 160 million years ago and from the Indian subcontinent around 88 million years ago. That long isolation let its plants and animals evolve independently, producing lemurs, the fossa, and several baobab species that exist on the island and nowhere else.

facts.claim: Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie were shot dead in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip.
facts.subject: the assassination that precipitated the First World War
facts.context: Princip was a South Slav nationalist. An associate had already thrown a bomb that bounced off the archduke's car earlier that morning; Princip shot the couple a short time later, as their car drove toward a hospital to visit the wounded.

facts.claim: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914, one month after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand.
facts.subject: the declaration of war that followed the Sarajevo assassination
facts.context: The assassination gave Austria-Hungary the pretext it had been seeking for hostilities against Serbia. The declaration triggered the alliance obligations that pulled Russia, Germany, France and Britain into the war within a week.

facts.claim: Archduke Franz Ferdinand was heir presumptive to the throne of Austria-Hungary at the time of his death.
facts.subject: Franz Ferdinand's position in the Austro-Hungarian succession
facts.context: He was nephew to Emperor Franz Joseph, and became heir after the deaths of the emperor's son and his own father. His marriage to Sophie Chotek was morganatic, meaning their children were barred from the succession.

facts.claim: The Colosseum in Rome was dedicated in 80 CE by the emperor Titus, with a hundred days of games.
facts.subject: the year the Colosseum in Rome was dedicated
facts.context: Construction began under Vespasian, Titus's father, on the drained site of the lake in Nero's Golden House. Vespasian died in 79 CE with the building unfinished, so it fell to Titus to open it. Ancient sources describe the inaugural games running a hundred days.

facts.claim: Measuring 189 by 156 metres and standing 45 metres high, the Colosseum is the largest amphitheatre built in the Roman world.
facts.subject: the largest amphitheatre built in the Roman world
facts.context: The measure is the footprint of the outer ellipse. Roman amphitheatres were free-standing ovals rather than hillside theatres, and several hundred were built across the empire; the one at Capua and the one at Verona are the nearest rivals in scale.

facts.claim: The Colosseum's fourth storey was added by the emperor Domitian in 82 CE, two years after the building was dedicated.
facts.subject: the emperor who added the Colosseum's fourth storey
facts.context: Domitian was the third and last of the Flavian emperors. The top storey he added was a wall pierced by small windows rather than an open arcade, and it carried the masts for the awning that shaded the seats.

facts.claim: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle in the Sea of Tranquility on 20 July 1969, while Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia.
facts.subject: the first crewed landing on the Moon
facts.context: The mission launched on 16 July 1969. Collins never walked on the Moon; his job was to keep Columbia flying and to perform the rendezvous that brought the other two home. The Sea of Tranquility is a basaltic lunar mare, chosen because it is comparatively flat.

facts.claim: The single Apollo 11 moonwalk lasted 2 hours and 31 minutes.
facts.subject: the duration of the Apollo 11 moonwalk
facts.context: Armstrong and Aldrin traversed about 250 metres in total and never went further than roughly 100 metres from the lunar module. Later Apollo crews stayed out far longer; Apollo 17 logged more than 22 hours of surface activity across three excursions.

facts.claim: Apollo 11 returned 21.55 kilograms of lunar rock and soil to Earth.
facts.subject: the mass of lunar material returned by Apollo 11
facts.context: About 48 pounds. The samples went to the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Houston within hours of splashdown, where the crew was also held in quarantine. Most of the Apollo sample collection is still held unopened so that future instruments can examine it.

facts.claim: Magna Carta was agreed by King John of England at Runnymede, near Windsor, on 15 June 1215.
facts.subject: the date Magna Carta was agreed at Runnymede
facts.context: A group of barons had rebelled against John's arbitrary rule and the heavy penalties he imposed on his subjects. Runnymede is a meadow on the Thames, neutral ground between the royal castle at Windsor and the rebel camp at Staines. Pope Innocent III annulled the charter ten weeks later, and it was reissued in revised form several times.

facts.claim: The Magna Carta agreed at Runnymede in 1215 contained 63 clauses.
facts.subject: the number of clauses in the 1215 Magna Carta
facts.context: Most of the 63 dealt with immediate baronial grievances about wardship, debts and forest law. Clauses 39 and 40, which forbid the sale of justice and require lawful judgement by one's peers, are the ones later generations built on.

facts.claim: Only three clauses of Magna Carta remain in force in English law: the liberties of the English church, the ancient liberties of the City of London, and the right to due legal process.
facts.subject: how much of Magna Carta is still law in England
facts.scope: clauses of Magna Carta not repealed from the statute book of England and Wales
facts.context: What survives on the statute book is the 1297 reissue by Edward I, not the 1215 charter. The rest was repealed piecemeal, most of it by the Statute Law Revision Acts of the nineteenth century. Two of the three surviving clauses protect institutions rather than individuals.

facts.claim: Construction of the Berlin Wall began in the early hours of 13 August 1961, when temporary barriers were put up along the border between the Soviet sector and West Berlin.
facts.subject: the date construction of the Berlin Wall began
facts.context: The first barriers were barbed wire and paving stones, not concrete. East Germany was losing roughly a thousand people a day through the open border in Berlin, which was the last gap in an otherwise sealed frontier. The concrete wall most people picture was the fourth generation, built from 1975.

facts.claim: The Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November 1989, 28 years, 2 months and 28 days after its construction began.
facts.subject: the date the Berlin Wall was opened
facts.context: Opening and demolition are different events. Crowds crossed freely from the night of 9 November, but systematic removal of the Wall ran through 1990 and into 1991. German reunification followed on 3 October 1990.

facts.claim: The Berlin Wall was opened after Guenter Schabowski told a press conference on 9 November 1989 that a new East German travel regime took effect immediately, when the announcement had in fact been intended for the following morning.
facts.subject: the East German official whose press conference opened the Berlin Wall
facts.context: Schabowski was a Politburo member who had not been at the meeting that drafted the rules and was reading from notes handed to him. West German television led its evening bulletin with the story, East Berliners went to the checkpoints in numbers, and the guards, with no orders, let them through.

facts.claim: The Titanic struck an iceberg late on 14 April 1912 and sank at 2:20 am on 15 April 1912, about 2 hours and 40 minutes after the collision.
facts.subject: the date the Titanic sank
facts.context: The collision and the sinking fall on different days, which is why sources write the date as 14 to 15 April. The iceberg opened at least five of the forward compartments; the ship was designed to stay afloat with four flooded.

facts.claim: The Titanic was on its maiden voyage from Southampton, England to New York City when it sank.
facts.subject: the Titanic's destination on its maiden voyage
facts.context: The ship called at Cherbourg in France and Queenstown, now Cobh, in Ireland before heading into the Atlantic. It was a British liner of the White Star Line, built in Belfast.

facts.claim: The Titanic carried 20 lifeboats, with space for 1,178 people, far short of the more than 2,200 on board.
facts.subject: the number of lifeboats the Titanic carried
facts.context: The ship carried more boats than Board of Trade regulations of the day required. Those rules were written around a ship's tonnage rather than the number of people aboard, and had not been revised as liners grew. Several boats were launched well under capacity.

facts.claim: Of the roughly 2,200 people aboard the Titanic, about 705 survived and around 1,500 died.
facts.subject: the number of people who survived the sinking of the Titanic
facts.context: Every figure here is approximate and sources disagree by a few dozen. The British and American inquiries counted differently, the passenger list was amended after sailing, and some crew were signed on under other names. Any question built on this fact should ask for an approximate figure, never an exact one.

facts.claim: Howard Carter discovered the tomb of Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings on 4 November 1922, after a seven-year search.
facts.subject: the archaeologist who discovered the tomb of Tutankhamun
facts.context: Discovery and opening are separate dates. What Carter's workmen uncovered on 4 November was the top step of a buried stairway; he waited for his sponsor Lord Carnarvon to arrive from England and broke through into the antechamber on 24 November. Asked whether he could see anything, Carter reportedly replied that he saw wonderful things.

facts.claim: Tutankhamun's tomb is designated KV62 in the Valley of the Kings and comprises four chambers.
facts.subject: the catalogue designation of Tutankhamun's tomb
facts.context: KV stands for Kings' Valley, and the numbers run in order of discovery rather than by reign. KV62 is small for a royal tomb, which is part of why it escaped the looting that emptied the larger ones, and why its contents survive nearly intact.

facts.claim: Tutankhamun came to the throne of Egypt at about nine years old and died at about nineteen, after a reign of roughly nine years.
facts.subject: Tutankhamun's age at death
facts.context: The nickname boy king comes from these numbers. The cause of death is not settled; disease and a badly broken leg are both proposed, and the older story of a blow to the head has been set aside by CT imaging of the mummy.

facts.claim: All sections of the Great Wall of China ever built total about 21,196 kilometres, or 13,171 miles, counting stretches that were rebuilt on the same ground.
facts.subject: the total length of the Great Wall of China
facts.context: The figure comes from a Chinese government survey and is a sum across dynasties, not the length of any one continuous wall. Earlier answers were far shorter because they counted only the Ming stretches then known. A question using this number should say which measure it means.

facts.claim: The Ming dynasty section of the Great Wall of China is about 8,850 kilometres long and is the best preserved.
facts.subject: the length of the Ming dynasty section of the Great Wall
facts.context: The Ming ruled from 1368 to 1644 and rebuilt the wall in brick and stone after the Mongol period. Nearly every photograph of the Great Wall shows Ming work, which is why this figure and the 21,196 kilometre total are so often confused.

facts.claim: The Great Wall of China is not visible to the naked eye from the Moon, and astronauts report it is difficult or impossible to pick out even from low Earth orbit.
facts.subject: whether the Great Wall of China can be seen from space with the naked eye
facts.context: The wall is long but narrow, a handful of metres wide, and built from local material that matches the ground around it. Width, not length, is what decides whether something can be resolved from orbit. Motorways and airport runways are wider and easier to see.

facts.claim: A Paris crowd stormed the Bastille on 14 July 1789, and the date is commemorated in France as Bastille Day.
facts.subject: the date the Bastille was stormed
facts.context: The fortress governor, Bernard-Rene Jordan de Launay, surrendered after a short fight and was killed by the crowd. France's national day marks this event rather than the declaration of the republic, which came three years later.

facts.claim: The Bastille held only seven inmates when it was stormed on 14 July 1789: four counterfeiters, two men confined as insane, and one count imprisoned at his family's request.
facts.subject: the number of prisoners held in the Bastille when it was stormed
facts.scope: every inmate held in the Bastille on 14 July 1789
facts.context: The fortress mattered as a symbol of arbitrary royal power rather than as a working prison. Louis XVI's government had already drawn up plans to demolish it as an expense not worth keeping.

facts.claim: The crowd that gathered at the Bastille on 14 July 1789 came to seize gunpowder and cannon, not to free the prisoners.
facts.subject: what the crowd at the Bastille came for on 14 July 1789
facts.context: About 900 Parisians assembled. The Bastille was where the city's powder stock was held, and the crowd wanted it for arms they had already collected. Negotiations with the governor failed, the crowd pushed into the inner courtyard, and the garrison opened fire.

facts.claim: China and Nepal jointly declared in December 2020 that Mount Everest stands 8,848.86 metres, or 29,031.69 feet, above sea level.
facts.subject: the official height of Mount Everest above sea level
facts.context: The figure came from parallel surveys run by both countries and was adopted by the National Geographic Society. Any older number a player remembers, most often 8,848 metres or 29,029 feet, is a superseded measurement rather than a wrong one.

facts.claim: Before the 2020 agreement China used a rock height for Mount Everest of 8,844.43 metres while Nepal used a snow height of 29,028 feet, the difference being whether the summit snowcap counts.
facts.subject: why China and Nepal long disagreed about the height of Mount Everest
facts.context: Rock height measures the bedrock under the ice; snow height measures the top of the snow. Neither is wrong, they answer different questions. The 2020 declaration settled on the snow height, which is why the agreed figure is the larger one.

facts.claim: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776.
facts.subject: the date the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence
facts.context: Congress had already voted for independence itself on 2 July, under the Lee Resolution. The 4th is the date the wording was approved, which is why John Adams expected 2 July to be the day Americans celebrated.

facts.claim: Delegates began signing the engrossed Declaration of Independence on 2 August 1776, not on 4 July, and 56 signed in all.
facts.subject: the date delegates began signing the Declaration of Independence
facts.context: Adoption and signing are different acts a month apart. John Hancock, president of the Congress, signed first and largest. Two delegates present for the vote, John Dickinson and Robert R. Livingston, never signed at all.

facts.claim: Thomas Jefferson wrote the draft of the Declaration of Independence, working between 11 and 28 June 1776 for a committee that also included John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Robert R. Livingston and Roger Sherman.
facts.subject: the principal author of the Declaration of Independence
facts.context: The group is known as the Committee of Five. Adams and Franklin marked up Jefferson's draft before it went to Congress, and Congress itself cut about a quarter of the text, including a passage attacking the slave trade.

facts.claim: Usain Bolt ran 9.58 seconds for 100 metres at the 2009 World Championships in Berlin, taking 0.11 seconds off his own previous record of 9.69.
facts.subject: Usain Bolt's fastest 100 metres
facts.context: The 9.69 he beat was his own, set at the Beijing Olympics almost exactly a year earlier, and he had eased up before the line in that race. A margin of 0.11 seconds is enormous in a sprint; the record had previously moved in hundredths.

facts.claim: As of September 2026, Usain Bolt's 9.58 seconds from 2009 remains the world record for the men's 100 metres.
facts.subject: the current world record for the men's 100 metres
facts.context: The record has stood over fifteen years. No one has come within a tenth of it since; the fastest men of the 2020s have run 9.76. This fact expires the moment somebody runs faster, so it should be rechecked before any use.

facts.claim: Brazil has won the FIFA World Cup five times, in 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994 and 2002, more than any other nation.
facts.subject: the country with the most FIFA World Cup titles
facts.context: Germany and Italy follow with four each. Spain's win in 2026 took it to two, level with Uruguay, France and Argentina. Brazil's last title was more than twenty years ago, so the lead is historical rather than current form.

facts.claim: Spain won the 2026 FIFA World Cup, beating Argentina 1-0 after extra time in the final on 19 July 2026, for its second title.
facts.subject: the winner of the 2026 FIFA World Cup
facts.context: The final was played at New York New Jersey Stadium before a crowd of more than 80,000, in the first World Cup hosted jointly by three countries: Canada, Mexico and the United States. Argentina were the defending champions and three-time winners.

facts.claim: Michael Jackson's Thriller is the best-selling album of all time by worldwide sales, at an estimated 67 million copies.
facts.subject: the best-selling album of all time by worldwide sales
facts.context: Worldwide sales is the measure that makes this true. On United States certification alone the answer is different, so a question asking simply which album sold the most has two defensible answers and should name the measure. Global totals before the 1990s are estimates in any case.

facts.claim: By RIAA certification in the United States, the Eagles' Their Greatest Hits 1971-1975 is the best-selling album at 38 times platinum, ahead of Thriller at 33 times platinum; it overtook Thriller in 2018.
facts.subject: the best-selling album in the United States by RIAA certification
facts.context: RIAA certification counts units shipped and, since 2016, streaming equivalents, which is not the same thing as copies sold worldwide. This is why the Eagles lead one list and Michael Jackson the other. Thriller remains the best-selling album in the United States by a solo artist.

facts.claim: Thriller was released on 30 November 1982 and was produced by Quincy Jones.
facts.subject: the release date of Michael Jackson's Thriller
facts.context: Jones had also produced Jackson's previous album, Off the Wall. The record is often dated to 1983 because that is when most of its singles and the long-form video reached their peak, but the album itself is a 1982 release.

facts.claim: Avatar, released in 2009, is the highest-grossing film of all time at the worldwide box office, with about 2.92 billion dollars.
facts.subject: the highest-grossing film of all time at the worldwide box office
facts.context: Avengers: Endgame is second at about 2.72 billion dollars and briefly held the top spot in 2019 before Avatar regained it through re-releases in 2021 and 2022. These are unadjusted figures; corrected for inflation the ranking changes completely.

facts.claim: Titanic, released in 1997, was the first film to take one billion dollars at the worldwide box office.
facts.subject: the first film to gross one billion dollars worldwide
facts.context: It held the all-time record until James Cameron's own Avatar passed it in 2010, and has since been overtaken by several other films. Being first past a milestone is a fixed fact; holding the record is not, which is why the two claims need separating.

facts.claim: Saturn has more confirmed moons than any other planet in the solar system, with 293 as of August 2026, against 115 for Jupiter.
facts.subject: the planet with the most confirmed moons
facts.context: Jupiter held this title for most of the space age. Saturn passed it in 2023 and the gap has widened since, because surveys keep turning up small irregular outer satellites a few kilometres across. Any specific count here goes out of date fast; the ordering is the durable part.

facts.claim: Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space, crossing the heliopause on 25 August 2012 at about 122 astronomical units from the Sun.
facts.subject: the first human-made object to enter interstellar space
facts.context: Launched in 1977, the probe had already flown past Jupiter and Saturn. The crossing was not seen at the time; it was established later from plasma density readings, which is why the announcement came a year after the date itself.

facts.claim: The heliopause is the boundary where the Sun's bubble of charged particles and magnetic field gives way to the interstellar medium, and crossing it is what counts as entering interstellar space.
facts.subject: the boundary that marks the edge of the Sun's influence
facts.context: It is not the edge of the solar system in the gravitational sense. The Oort cloud, still bound to the Sun, extends far beyond it, and Voyager 1 will take many thousands of years to pass through that.

facts.claim: In 1998 two independent teams studying distant Type Ia supernovae found that the expansion of the universe is accelerating rather than slowing down.
facts.subject: what two teams of astronomers discovered about the universe in 1998
facts.answer: The expansion of the universe is accelerating
facts.context: The supernovae came out fainter, and therefore further away, than a universe slowing under its own gravity would allow. Everyone had expected to measure how fast the slowing was. Two teams working separately, the Supernova Cosmology Project and the High-z Supernova Search Team, reached the same answer, which is why it was believed so quickly.

facts.claim: The 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess for the discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe.
facts.subject: the physicists awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize for the accelerating universe
facts.answer: Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess
facts.context: Perlmutter led the Supernova Cosmology Project; Schmidt led the High-z team with Riess doing much of the analysis. The prize was for establishing the acceleration, not for explaining it. Dark energy is a name for the unknown cause, not a solution to it.

facts.claim: The James Webb Space Telescope observes from about 0.6 to 28 microns, reaching into the mid-infrared, while Hubble covers 0.1 to 2.5 microns, from ultraviolet to the near-infrared.
facts.subject: the wavelengths the James Webb Space Telescope observes compared with Hubble
facts.context: The extra infrared reach is the point of the telescope. Light from the earliest galaxies is stretched by the expansion of the universe into wavelengths Hubble cannot see, and infrared also passes through the dust that hides star-forming regions in visible light.

facts.claim: The James Webb Space Telescope's segmented primary mirror is 6.5 metres across and collects almost six times more light than Hubble's 2.4 metre mirror.
facts.subject: the size of the James Webb Space Telescope's primary mirror
facts.context: The mirror is built from 18 hexagonal segments because a single 6.5 metre disc would not fit in any launch vehicle; it was folded for launch and unfolded in space. Webb sits at Lagrange point 2, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth, where its sunshield can keep the Sun, Earth and Moon all on one side.

facts.claim: The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest point on Earth's land surface, about 430 metres below sea level in the mid-2010s and still falling.
facts.subject: the lowest point on Earth's land surface
facts.context: The number moves. The level was near 400 metres below sea level in the mid-twentieth century and has dropped steadily since, because the Jordan river and other tributaries are diverted for irrigation and because of evaporation works in the south. Any figure quoted for this should be given as approximate and dated.

facts.claim: The Dead Sea's eastern shore is in Jordan, the southern half of its western shore is in Israel, and the northern half of the western shore is in the West Bank.
facts.subject: the territories bordering the Dead Sea
facts.answer: Jordan, Israel and the West Bank
facts.scope: every territory with shoreline on the Dead Sea
facts.context: A question asking which two countries border the Dead Sea has no clean answer, because the third stretch of shoreline is the West Bank rather than a recognised sovereign state. Either name all three, or ask which country holds the eastern shore, which is unambiguous.

facts.claim: Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address on 19 November 1863, at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania.
facts.subject: the president who delivered the Gettysburg Address
facts.context: The battle had been fought there the previous July. Lincoln was not the main speaker and the address was not the reason for the ceremony; he was invited to add a few appropriate remarks after the formal oration.

facts.claim: Lincoln's Gettysburg Address lasted about two minutes, following a two-hour oration by Edward Everett.
facts.subject: how long the Gettysburg Address took to deliver
facts.context: Everett was the most celebrated orator in the country and was the day's featured speaker. He wrote to Lincoln afterwards to say the short speech had come closer to the heart of the occasion than his own long one. Several manuscript copies in Lincoln's hand survive and their wording differs slightly.

facts.claim: The Dead Sea has fallen about 45 metres over the past fifty years, and the rate of decline has risen from 17 centimetres a year between 1930 and 1973 to about a metre a year by the turn of the century.
facts.subject: how fast the Dead Sea is shrinking
facts.answer: About 45 metres over the past fifty years
facts.context: The cause is upstream diversion of the Jordan river for irrigation and municipal water, together with mineral extraction that evaporates water in the southern basin. As the level drops, groundwater dissolves buried salt layers and sinkholes open along the exposed shoreline.

facts.claim: LeBron James is the leading scorer in NBA regular-season history, closing the 2025-26 season with 43,440 career points.
facts.subject: the leading scorer in NBA regular-season history
facts.context: He was still playing when this was recorded, so the total is a floor rather than a final figure. He also leads the playoff scoring list at 8,289 points and is the only player past 50,000 points across both. Any question using a specific total needs a season attached to it.

facts.claim: LeBron James broke Kareem Abdul-Jabbar's NBA career regular-season scoring record.
facts.subject: the player whose NBA career scoring record LeBron James broke
facts.context: Passing a record is a fixed event; holding it is not, which is why this and the current-total fact are kept separate. The exact date and Abdul-Jabbar's final total are not carried by the sources cited here and need their own check before a question uses them.

facts.claim: Barry Bonds holds the Major League Baseball career home run record with 762.
facts.subject: the holder of the Major League Baseball career home run record
facts.context: He passed Hank Aaron's 755 on 7 August 2007 with his 756th, then hit six more before retiring. Aaron's record had stood 33 years. Bonds played 22 seasons, for the Pittsburgh Pirates and then the San Francisco Giants.

facts.claim: Barry Bonds also holds the Major League Baseball single-season home run record, with 73 in 2001.
facts.subject: the Major League Baseball single-season home run record
facts.context: Career and single-season are different records that happen to be held by the same man, which makes them easy to confuse in a question. Bonds set the 73 in the same era as several other assaults on the single-season mark.

facts.claim: Emmitt Smith became the NFL's all-time leading rusher on 27 October 2002, passing Walter Payton's 16,726 yards with an 11-yard run that took him to 16,728.
facts.subject: the player who broke Walter Payton's NFL career rushing record
facts.context: Payton, nicknamed Sweetness, had held the record for 18 years. Smith was 33 and playing for the Dallas Cowboys against Seattle at home in Irving, Texas. He broke it in the fourth quarter by two yards.

facts.claim: The maximum break in a single frame of snooker is 147, made by potting each of the 15 reds with a black and then clearing the six colours in sequence.
facts.subject: the maximum break in a single frame of snooker
facts.context: The arithmetic is 15 reds at one point each plus 15 blacks at seven, which is 120, then yellow through black in order for another 27. Higher breaks are possible in a frame only through a free ball after a foul, which is a different situation from the standard maximum.

facts.claim: The first officially recognised maximum break of 147 in professional snooker was made by Steve Davis in 1982 at the Lada Classic.
facts.subject: the first player to make an officially recognised 147 break
facts.context: Maximums were rare for decades after that and have become far more common as the standard of play has risen. The World Snooker Tour keeps an official register of them.

facts.claim: The Nile is conventionally given as the world's longest river, at about 6,650 kilometres or 4,132 miles, and the United States Geological Survey puts it roughly 100 miles longer than the Amazon.
facts.subject: the river conventionally given as the world's longest
facts.context: This is the standard answer and the one most reference works give, but it is not settled. River lengths are hard to compare because countries define stream courses and measurement standards differently. A question using this should accept the convention rather than present it as beyond dispute.

facts.claim: A 2007 Brazilian study measured the Amazon at 6,992 kilometres against 6,853 kilometres for the Nile, making the Amazon the longer river by its reckoning.
facts.subject: the study that found the Amazon longer than the Nile
facts.context: The result depends entirely on two choices. The team took Apacheta Creek in Peru as the Amazon's source, and the south side of Marajo Island as its mouth, which alone added 353 kilometres. That second choice is contested. Both the Amazon's length and its ultimate source have been argued over since the mid-twentieth century.

facts.claim: A desert is defined by precipitation rather than temperature, conventionally as an area receiving less than 250 millimetres of precipitation a year.
facts.subject: what makes an area a desert
facts.answer: Less than 250 millimetres of precipitation a year
facts.context: Heat has nothing to do with it. Some authorities put the line at 25 centimetres and count areas up to 40 centimetres as semidesert. Polar deserts are a recognised type in their own right, occurring over ice near both poles.

facts.claim: By the precipitation definition of a desert, the largest desert on Earth is the Antarctic Ice Sheet, at about 13,960,000 square kilometres, not the Sahara.
facts.subject: the largest desert on Earth by area
facts.context: Reference works disagree here, and both answers are defensible depending on the convention used: Antarctica is the largest desert of any kind, the Sahara the largest hot desert. A question asking simply for the largest desert has two correct answers and should name which it means.

facts.claim: Antarctica's inland polar plateau receives about 50 millimetres of precipitation a year, almost all of it as snow, while the coastal belt receives perhaps 500 millimetres.
facts.subject: how much precipitation Antarctica receives
facts.answer: About 50 millimetres of precipitation a year
facts.context: That inland figure is drier than most hot deserts. The interior of the ice sheet gets under 5 centimetres a year. Snow that falls there does not melt, so the ice accumulates over millennia despite the tiny annual input.

facts.claim: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, making up about 74 percent of all matter, with helium next at about 24 percent.
facts.subject: the most abundant element in the universe
facts.context: Between them the two lightest elements account for roughly 98 percent of ordinary matter, and everything heavier is the remainder. Both were made in the first minutes after the Big Bang; the heavier elements came later, inside stars.

facts.claim: Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust, at about 46 percent of its mass.
facts.subject: the most abundant element in Earth's crust
facts.context: Almost none of it is the free oxygen we breathe. It is locked into silicate minerals and oxides, bound to silicon, aluminium and iron. Crust, whole Earth, and universe give three different answers to a question about the most abundant element, so the question has to say which.

facts.claim: Hydrogen makes up only about 0.14 percent of Earth's crust by weight, despite being the most abundant element in the universe.
facts.subject: how much of Earth's crust is hydrogen
facts.context: The young Earth was too warm and too small to hold onto light gases, so most of its hydrogen and helium escaped. What remains is mostly bound up in water and in hydrated minerals rather than present as the free gas.

facts.claim: India is the world's most populous country, having overtaken China in April 2023.
facts.subject: the world's most populous country
facts.context: China had held the position for as long as records allowed the comparison. India's population is projected to keep growing for decades while China's peaked and began falling in 2022, so the gap is widening rather than closing. Any question written before 2023 will have the old answer.

facts.claim: The Second World War began in Europe on 1 September 1939, when Germany invaded Poland, and Britain and France declared war two days later.
facts.subject: the date the Second World War began in Europe
facts.context: The phrase in Europe is doing work here. Fighting between Japan and China had been under way since 1937, and some histories date the war from there. The European start date is the conventional one.

facts.claim: The Second World War ended with Japan's formal surrender on 2 September 1945.
facts.subject: the date the Second World War ended
facts.context: Germany had surrendered nearly four months earlier, on 8 May, which is why VE Day and the end of the war are different dates. The formal Japanese surrender was signed aboard a warship in Tokyo Bay, after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki that August.

facts.claim: Canada has the world's longest coastline, at 243,042 kilometres, counting the mainland coast together with the coasts of its offshore islands.
facts.subject: the country with the world's longest coastline
facts.context: The islands are most of it. Canada's Arctic archipelago contributes far more shoreline than the mainland does, which is why the total dwarfs that of any other country. Coastline figures depend on the scale of measurement, so the source matters: this is the Statistics Canada figure.

facts.claim: Canada has more lake area than any other country, with 563 lakes larger than 100 square kilometres and 891,163 square kilometres of fresh water in total.
facts.subject: the country with the most lake area
facts.context: The often-repeated line that Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined is a different and much stronger claim, and the official Canadian sources do not make it. What they document is lake area and count of large lakes. A question should use the sourced version.

facts.claim: The Amazon Rainforest is the world's largest tropical rainforest, covering about 6,000,000 square kilometres.
facts.subject: the world's largest tropical rainforest
facts.context: It occupies the drainage basin of the Amazon river and its tributaries, bounded by the Guiana Highlands to the north, the Andes to the west, the Brazilian central plateau to the south and the Atlantic to the east.

facts.claim: Brazil holds about 60 percent of the Amazon Rainforest, which in turn makes up about 40 percent of Brazil's total area.
facts.subject: the share of the Amazon Rainforest that lies in Brazil
facts.context: The other 40 percent is spread across eight further countries and one overseas territory, chiefly Peru and Colombia. The two percentages in this fact point in opposite directions and are easy to swap in a question: 60 percent of the forest is in Brazil, 40 percent of Brazil is forest.

facts.claim: The Pantanal is the world's largest tropical wetland, covering about 42 million acres across Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay.
facts.subject: the world's largest tropical wetland
facts.context: Most of it lies in Brazil, but it is not contained by any one country. Floodwaters fill it from October to March and drain slowly from April to September, and that annual cycle is what sustains its wildlife. It holds more than 4,700 recorded plant and animal species.

facts.claim: Uruguay won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930, beating Argentina 4-2 in the final on home soil as hosts.
facts.subject: the winner of the first FIFA World Cup
facts.context: The tournament ran from 13 to 30 July 1930. Uruguay both hosted and won, a double repeated only a handful of times since. Many European teams declined to make the sea crossing, so the field was small by later standards.

facts.claim: Pele won three World Cups with Brazil, in 1958, 1962 and 1970.
facts.subject: the number of World Cups Pele won with Brazil
facts.context: No other player has won three. He was 17 at the first of them and injured for most of the 1962 tournament, which is sometimes raised as an asterisk, though he played in the group stage and holds the winner's medal.

facts.claim: The Jules Rimet Trophy was the World Cup prize from 1930 to 1970 and was awarded permanently to Brazil in 1970 after its third win.
facts.subject: the original World Cup trophy
facts.context: It was named for the FIFA president who proposed the tournament. The rule was that a third title won the trophy outright, which Brazil achieved in 1970. A new trophy has been used since 1974 and is not given away.

facts.claim: Easter Island is a dependency of Chile, lying about 3,500 kilometres west of the Chilean mainland in the eastern Pacific.
facts.subject: the country Easter Island belongs to
facts.context: The island's Polynesian name is Rapa Nui, and Rapa Nui National Park is a World Heritage property. The distance is what makes it one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth, far closer to Polynesia culturally than to South America.

facts.claim: Easter Island holds over 600 moai, carved from tuff quarried in the crater walls of the volcano Rano Raraku, most of them between 10 and 20 feet tall.
facts.subject: the stone statues of Easter Island
facts.context: Counts vary by source and by what is being counted: finished statues raised on platforms, or those plus the hundreds left unfinished in the quarry. Figures near 900 or a thousand come from counting the quarry. The largest ever raised on a platform stood about 32 feet. They are thought to represent ancestors.

facts.claim: The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is the driest non-polar desert on Earth, running 1,000 to 1,100 kilometres north to south, with mean annual precipitation under 1 millimetre in its driest parts.
facts.subject: the driest non-polar desert on Earth
facts.context: The qualifier non-polar is necessary: the Antarctic dry valleys are drier still. Some Atacama weather stations have never recorded rain at all, and parts of the desert see rainfall only two to four times a century.

facts.claim: Cape Horn is a rocky headland on Hornos Island in the Tierra del Fuego archipelago of southern Chile, and is not technically the southernmost point of South America.
facts.subject: what and where Cape Horn is
facts.answer: A rocky headland on Hornos Island
facts.context: It is an island headland, not a point on the mainland, and the Diego Ramirez islands lie further south again. Its reputation comes from the sailing route around it rather than from any geographical record. A question calling it the southernmost tip of South America is overstating it.

facts.claim: Julius Caesar was assassinated in the Roman Senate House on 15 March 44 BC by a group of nobles led by Gaius Cassius Longinus and Marcus Junius Brutus.
facts.subject: the assassination of Julius Caesar
facts.context: Some 60 men were reportedly in the conspiracy. Caesar had recently been made dictator for life, which is what turned senatorial resentment into a plot. The killing did not restore the republic; it began the civil wars that ended with Augustus as emperor.

facts.claim: The Ides of March is 15 March in the ancient Roman calendar.
facts.subject: the date of the Ides of March
facts.context: Ides fell on the 15th in March, May, July and October, and on the 13th in the other months, so the Ides are not always mid-month in the modern sense. The association with doom comes from Caesar's death and from Shakespeare's play about it.

facts.claim: Napoleon was finally defeated at the Battle of Waterloo on 18 June 1815, by the Duke of Wellington's allied army together with a Prussian army under Gebhard Leberecht von Blucher.
facts.subject: the battle at which Napoleon was finally defeated
facts.context: The battle was fought south of Waterloo in what is now Belgium. It took two armies, not one: Wellington held the ridge through the afternoon and Blucher's Prussians arrived on the French flank late in the day. It ended 23 years of recurrent war between France and the other European powers.

facts.claim: Napoleon abdicated as emperor of France on 22 June 1815, four days after Waterloo, and was exiled to St Helena.
facts.subject: what happened to Napoleon after Waterloo
facts.context: It was his second and final abdication; the first had come in 1814 and sent him to Elba, from which he returned. St Helena is a remote South Atlantic island, chosen precisely so that no second return was possible. He died there in 1821.

facts.claim: Michael Phelps won 28 Olympic medals, 23 of them gold, more than any other athlete in Olympic history.
facts.subject: the athlete with the most Olympic medals
facts.context: His gold tally is more than double that of his nearest rival. The total came across four Games: Athens, Beijing, London and Rio, the last after he had already announced his retirement.

facts.claim: Michael Phelps won eight gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, every event he entered, breaking Mark Spitz's record of seven at a single Games set in 1972.
facts.subject: the most gold medals won at a single Olympic Games
facts.context: He also set world records in seven of the eight. Spitz's seven had stood for 36 years. This single-Games record and Phelps's career medal total are separate facts and are easily confused in a question.

facts.claim: Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on 1 January 1863, having issued a preliminary proclamation on 22 September 1862 warning that enslaved people in areas still in rebellion would be declared free.
facts.subject: the president who issued the Emancipation Proclamation
facts.context: There are two documents and two dates. The preliminary proclamation of September 1862 set the deadline; the final one of January 1863 carried it out. Questions asking when it was signed can mean either.

facts.claim: The Emancipation Proclamation applied only to areas in rebellion against the Union and left slavery untouched in the loyal border states of Maryland, Kentucky and Missouri.
facts.subject: the limits of what the Emancipation Proclamation freed
facts.answer: Areas in rebellion against the Union
facts.context: It was framed as a military measure, which is why its reach stopped where Union authority already ran. Slavery was ended everywhere in the United States by the Thirteenth Amendment, not by this proclamation. The document also opened the Union Army and Navy to Black men, and almost 200,000 had served by the war's end.
